articles.title: Country diary: The multitudinous mysteries of grassland | Paul Evans
articles.description: The Marches, Shropshire: From the millions of glinting spiders’ webs to patches of slime-mould, I find the rain-soaked grass is teeming with life From here, I walk across a field wet with last night’s rain. It’s like walking through water. The sun is sinking, scattering shards of brilliance over the grass. The field glitters around sheep, eating grass, dunging grass, attending to the ancient ways of grass. It’s tupping time and these ewes and rams (tups) are sparking the conception of next year’s lambs that will gambol in the spring grass as they have for centuries. It reminds me of a story that a farmer told me about a visit from a Defra inspector who asked him how many sheep he had: “One hundred and thirty-five,” replied the farmer. “If I count any more than that I go to sleep.” From here, last week, I walked through scattered patches of dog vomit slime mould, Mucilago crustacea, sticking to the tips of grass blades. They begin like sulphur, then turn to gluey tapioca, their tiny spore-bearing granules opening black after a day or so, and then they vanish into the mysteries of the sward. From here, the week before, I walked into fog hung with the ochres of spectral trees, with only the grass underfoot visible, as if the field were high in the clouds above. Continue reading...

articles.title: Chad: DIEM-Monitoring emergency agriculture support brief, September 2026 (round 10)
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Synopsis (short abstract) This emergency agriculture support brief presents the results of the Data in Emergencies Monitoring (DIEM-Monitoring) survey conducted in Chad in July and August 2026. Data analysis estimated that 67 131 resident agricultural households (447 012 people) required emergency food security assistance in the six provinces covered by the survey. This brief provides humanitarian actors with a detailed analysis of the needs of agricultural households to better target interventions aimed at supporting their livelihoods, strengthening their resilience to future shocks and safeguarding the food security of rural populations. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) established DIEM-Monitoring in June 2020. DIEM enumerators collect data several times a year across food-insecure countries, through computer-assisted telephone interviews and face-to-face surveys. These data cover shocks, agricultural livelihoods, food security and household needs, and are regularly updated and easily accessible on the DIEM Hub. DIEM products consist of dashboards, maps, briefs and aggregated data, enabling partners and stakeholders to activate mitigation measures and target vulnerable households.

articles.title: World: Crop Monitor for AMIS | No. 144 – November 2026
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Overview At the end of October, overall conditions are positive for wheat, maize, rice, and soybeans. Wheat conditions are generally favourable; winter wheat continues to develop in the Southern Hemisphere, and sowing continues in the Northern Hemisphere. Maize conditions are favourable, as harvest progresses in the Northern Hemisphere and sowing expands in the Southern Hemisphere. Rice conditions are favourable, with harvest ongoing in China and for India’s Kharif season. Soybean harvesting is continuing in the Northern Hemisphere, with good yields expected in the US and poor yields in Europe. Crop Conditions at a Glance Wheat – Conditions are generally favourable in the Southern Hemisphere as harvesting begins. In the Northern Hemisphere, winter wheat sowing is progressing. Maize – Harvesting is progressing in the Northern Hemisphere as sowing picks up pace in the Southern Hemisphere. Rice – Harvesting is progressing in China and for India’s Kharif season, along with wet-season rice in northern Southeast Asia and dry-season rice in southern Southeast Asia. Soybeans – In the Northern Hemisphere, the harvest is wrapping up under poor conditions in Europe, while exceptional in the US. Forecasts at a Glance Climate Influences – Strong El Niño conditions are present and strengthening. The event will likely be very strong and rank among the strongest since 1950. El Niño conditions are forecast through April 2027 (98% chance). A positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) event is underway and forecast through December. Europe - During November-December-January 2026/27, precipitation is likely to be above-average across much of Europe, while temperatures are also likely to be above-average. South Africa - The November–December–January (NDJ) 2026/27 forecast indicates drier and warmer-than-average conditions, which will likely negatively impact crops. United States – The November forecast supports the likely improvement or removal of drought conditions across large portions of the southern and western US.

articles.title: World: GEOGLAM Global Crop Monitor | No. 49 – November 2026
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Global Crop Overview Global crop conditions at the end of October are generally positive for wheat, maize, rice, and soybeans. Wheat conditions are generally favourable as harvesting begins in the Southern Hemisphere and winter wheat sowing progresses in the Northern Hemisphere. Maize conditions are generally favourable, though yields are poor in Europe, parts of East Africa, and the US. Rice conditions are generally favourable; however, adverse weather is negatively impacting crops in parts of Southeast Asia. Soybean harvesting is ongoing in the Northern Hemisphere, with good yields expected in the US, poor yields in Europe, and mixed outcomes in India. Sowing is ongoing in Brazil. The CM4EW publication discusses the remaining crops. Global Climate Influences Overview Strong El Niño conditions are present and strengthening. The event will likely be very strong and rank among the strongest since 1950. El Niño conditions are forecast through April 2027 (98% chance). A positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) event is underway and forecast through December. During late October through early November 2026, abnormally hot temperatures are forecast in active crop development areas of southern and eastern Mexico, Central America, Haiti, central Brazil, southern West Africa, Sudan, Somalia, Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe, northern Mozambique, northern South Africa, Pakistan, western and southern India, and parts of Southeast Asia. For further details on the Global Climate Influences and Regional Climate Outlooks section.
